executive_summary: The commenter urges CMS to distinguish mere API conformance and usage from true interoperability completeness. They recommend oversight that evaluates whether payer-maintained USCDI data used for payment, risk adjustment, quality measurement, utilization management, or care management is also available through CMS-required interoperability APIs, while minimizing burden by leveraging existing audit and validation activities.

detailed_positions.rationale: API availability, transaction volume, and attestations do not prove that all payer-maintained clinical/USCDI data is accessible through APIs.
detailed_positions.specific_request: Future oversight should evaluate whether USCDI data exchanged between covered entities and maintained or used by payers is accessible through CMS-required APIs.

detailed_positions.rationale: New reporting programs could add administrative burden; existing audit and validation programs already review completeness, accuracy, and provenance of operational data.
detailed_positions.specific_request: Leverage quality measurement and risk adjustment validation activities to assess whether payer-held USCDI data is available through APIs.

solicitation_responses.summary: Responds indirectly to API usage metrics by arguing that activity and conformance metrics are insufficient unless paired with completeness/accountability measures.
General oversight recommendation to evaluate interoperability completeness while minimizing burden through existing audit programs.

recommendations: Distinguish API conformance/activity from interoperability completeness.
Assess whether payer-maintained USCDI data used for operational purposes is available through CMS-required APIs.
Avoid creating wholly new reporting programs where existing audit/validation activities can be leveraged.
Use quality measurement and risk adjustment validation frameworks to evaluate data completeness and provenance.

primary_concerns: Payers may technically conform while excluding externally sourced or operationally used USCDI data from APIs.
API volume metrics may not measure whether APIs meet patient/provider data needs.
potential_negative_impacts_cited: Incomplete patient/provider access to payer-maintained clinical data; misleading compliance metrics.
implementation_barriers_mentioned: Need to identify payer-maintained data, provenance, and whether it should be exposed through APIs without adding duplicative reporting burdens.

examples_provided: Clinical data used for payment, quality measurement, risk adjustment, utilization management, and care management may not be exposed through APIs.

impact_assessment.economic_implications: Could avoid duplicative administrative reporting if tied to existing audits; may require more robust payer data mapping and validation.
impact_assessment.technical_feasibility: Feasible if CMS defines completeness expectations and leverages existing validation processes.
impact_assessment.patient_care_impact: Greater completeness could improve patient access, provider access, and reuse of data for treatment and related interoperability purposes.

key_quotes: CMS oversight should distinguish API conformance and activity from interoperability completeness.

API availability, transaction volume, and attestation metrics may provide useful operational information, but they do not necessarily measure whether all payer-maintained USCDI data is actually available.

The long-term success of nationwide interoperability will depend not only on whether APIs exist and are used, but also on whether data exchanged to support payer operational processes is also available.
